title: Cardinality and participation constraints
description: A practical guide to specifying relationship multiplicity and mandatory participation in a relational model, using a hypothetical retail dataset with counterexamples and diagnostic SQL.
lead: Cardinality and participation constraints answer two different questions that are often collapsed into one drawing. Cardinality says how many related rows are allowed. Participation says whether a related row is required. A useful relational model states both.

sections.heading: Two questions, not one
paragraphs: When practitioners say a customer has many orders, they are usually talking about maximum cardinality: more than one order may reference the same customer. That statement is incomplete. It does not say whether every order must have a customer, whether every customer must have at least one order, or whether an order may exist before its lines are loaded.

A relationship specification should answer both the maximum and the minimum question on each side. Maximum cardinality gives the familiar one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many patterns. Minimum participation gives the required or optional part: zero allowed, or at least one required.

A compact way to write this is min..max beside each entity in the relationship. For example, Customer 0..* to Order 1..1 means a customer may have zero or many orders, while each order must reference exactly one customer. The first side is optional participation with many maximum cardinality. The second side is mandatory participation with one maximum cardinality.
The SQL examples use PostgreSQL 18 syntax. The modeling discussion concerns relationship rules; index choices, optimizer behavior, and physical tuning are outside its scope.
bullets: Cardinality: the maximum number of related rows allowed.
Participation: the minimum number of related rows required.
A complete relationship statement includes both sides: left min..max and right min..max.
A foreign key alone does not describe every participation rule in the conceptual model.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail model
paragraphs: Assume a small hypothetical retail-order dataset with customers, orders, order items, products, and customer profiles. The business rules are deliberately small enough to inspect by hand.

The first relationship is Customer to RetailOrder. A customer may have placed no orders yet, or may have placed many orders. Every order must belong to exactly one customer. Written as min..max: Customer 0..* to RetailOrder 1..1.

The second relationship is RetailOrder to OrderItem. Every order must contain at least one item. Every item belongs to exactly one order. Written as min..max: RetailOrder 1..* to OrderItem 1..1. This rule is more interesting because the mandatory side points from parent to child: the parent row is not complete unless at least one child row exists.

The third relationship is Customer to CustomerProfile. A customer may have no profile, but may not have more than one. Every profile belongs to exactly one customer. Written as min..max: Customer 0..1 to CustomerProfile 1..1.

The fourth relationship is Product to OrderItem. A product may appear in zero or many order items. Every order item must identify exactly one product. Written as min..max: Product 0..* to OrderItem 1..1.
bullets: Customer 0..* to RetailOrder 1..1: optional participation for customers, mandatory participation for orders.
RetailOrder 1..* to OrderItem 1..1: mandatory participation on both sides, with many items allowed per order.
Customer 0..1 to CustomerProfile 1..1: at most one profile per customer, and no orphan profile.
Product 0..* to OrderItem 1..1: products can exist before they sell, but order items cannot exist without a product.

sections.heading: What the relational constraints enforce
paragraphs: The DDL above enforces several relationship rules directly. The NOT NULL foreign key on retail_order.customer_id says an order must name a customer. The referenced primary key says the named customer must exist. Together they enforce the RetailOrder 1..1 side of Customer to RetailOrder.

The model also allows many orders per customer because customer_id is not unique in retail_order. If a unique constraint were added to retail_order.customer_id, the design would accidentally become Customer 0..1 to RetailOrder 1..1. That would reject a second order from the same customer, contradicting the intended rule.

The customer_profile table uses customer_id as both primary key and foreign key. That pattern enforces at most one profile per customer, because the primary key permits only one row for a given customer_id. It also enforces that every profile belongs to an existing customer. It does not require every customer to have a profile; that is intentional in this example.

The order_item primary key allows several lines per order because line_no varies within order_id. The NOT NULL foreign key to retail_order enforces that each item belongs to one existing order. The NOT NULL foreign key to product enforces that each item names one existing product.

One rule is not fully enforced by these ordinary row-level constraints: every order must have at least one item. The foreign key from order_item to retail_order prevents orphan items. It does not prevent a parent order from existing with no children. That is the common trap: a child-to-parent mandatory rule is easy to express with NOT NULL plus foreign key; a parent-to-child mandatory rule usually needs a different lifecycle control, validation query, deferred constraint mechanism, trigger, stored procedure, or application transaction boundary.
bullets: NOT NULL on a foreign key expresses mandatory participation from child to parent.
A non-unique foreign key permits many children for the same parent.
A UNIQUE constraint or primary key on a foreign key can express at-most-one on the child table.
A plain foreign key does not guarantee that every parent has at least one child.

sections.heading: Counterexamples in the data
paragraphs: Counterexamples make the distinction visible. The following rows are hypothetical and are meant as a staging or review fixture, not as a claim about any real retailer. Some rows should be accepted by the model; others illustrate specific violations.

Customers 1, 2, and 3 are valid customers. Customer 1 has two orders, which is allowed because the relationship is one customer to many orders. Customer 3 has no orders, which is also allowed because customer participation in orders is optional in this example.

Order 103 has a missing customer_id. That violates mandatory participation from RetailOrder to Customer. Order 104 references customer 999, which is also invalid because the required parent does not exist. Order 101 has no order items. That violates the business rule RetailOrder 1..* to OrderItem, even though a simple order table row could exist unless the load process prevents it.

The duplicate profile for customer 1 violates the at-most-one side of Customer 0..1 to CustomerProfile. A profile for customer 4 violates the mandatory parent rule for profiles, because there is no customer 4 in the customer table.
bullets: Valid: customer 1 has orders 100 and 101.
Valid: customer 3 has zero orders.
Invalid: order 103 has no customer.
Invalid: order 104 references a non-existent customer.
Invalid: order 101 has zero items.
Invalid: customer 1 has two profile rows.
Invalid: customer profile 4 has no matching customer.

codeExamples.code:
INSERT INTO customer (customer_id, customer_name) VALUES
    (1, 'Asha'),
    (2, 'Ben'),
    (3, 'Cy');

INSERT INTO product (product_id, sku, product_name) VALUES
    (10, 'MUG-BLUE', 'Blue mug'),
    (11, 'TEA-250G', 'Tea 250g');

INSERT INTO retail_order (order_id, customer_id, placed_at) VALUES
    (100, 1, timestamp '2026-09-28 09:00:00'),
    (101, 1, timestamp '2026-09-28 09:05:00'),
    (102, 2, timestamp '2026-09-28 09:10:00');

INSERT INTO order_item (order_id, line_no, product_id, quantity) VALUES
    (100, 1, 10, 1),
    (100, 2, 11, 2),
    (102, 1, 10, 1);

INSERT INTO customer_profile (customer_id, marketing_email, created_at) VALUES
    (1, 'asha@example.invalid', timestamp '2026-09-28 08:00:00'),
    (2, 'ben@example.invalid', timestamp '2026-09-28 08:10:00');

sections.heading: Diagnostic queries for staging and audits
paragraphs: In a production schema with enforced constraints, some violations cannot persist. In staging tables, lakehouse bronze tables, imports, reverse-engineering exercises, and data contracts, diagnostics are still useful. They make the intended relationship semantics executable as checks.

The first diagnostic finds orders that do not have exactly one valid customer. In a constrained relational table, NOT NULL plus foreign key should prevent these rows. In staging data, the query makes the rule explicit.

The second diagnostic finds orders with no items. This is the parent-to-child mandatory participation rule that ordinary foreign keys do not fully capture. If the business rule says an order is not valid until it has at least one item, this query identifies incomplete orders.

The third diagnostic finds customers with more than one profile in a staging table. In the final schema, customer_profile.customer_id as a primary key prevents duplicates. In raw data, grouping by customer_id exposes the violation before loading.

These diagnostics should not be confused with performance recommendations. A large system may need indexes, partition-aware checks, incremental validation, or data quality tooling. Those choices belong to physical implementation. The modeling step is to state the rule precisely enough that any implementation can be judged against it.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN customer AS c
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL
   OR c.customer_id IS NULL;

SELECT
    o.order_id
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN order_item AS i
    ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id
HAVING COUNT(i.order_id) = 0;

SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS profile_count
FROM customer_profile_staging
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

sections.heading: A checklist for specifying both constraints
paragraphs: A practical model review can be short. For each relationship, name the two entities, choose the parent and child if the relationship is directional in the schema, then write min..max on both sides. Do not stop at one-to-many. The minimum is where many production data quality surprises hide.

Next, classify which parts are enforceable with ordinary relational constraints. Primary keys identify rows. Foreign keys require referenced parents. NOT NULL makes a reference mandatory. UNIQUE and primary key constraints limit multiplicity. CHECK constraints handle row-local facts such as positive quantity, but they do not count related rows in another table.

Finally, decide how to handle rules that cross rows or require existence of children. For an order that must have at least one item, common choices include creating orders and items in the same transaction, preventing an order from reaching a submitted status until lines exist, using a deferred database mechanism, or running a validation job before publishing curated data. The right choice depends on lifecycle semantics, not just DDL elegance.

The most important modeling habit is to state the intended valid and invalid examples. If the team cannot agree whether customer 3 with zero orders is valid, or whether order 101 with zero items is valid, the diagram is not specific enough.
bullets: Write each relationship as EntityA min..max to EntityB min..max.
Translate maximum one into primary key or unique constraints where appropriate.
Translate mandatory child-to-parent participation into NOT NULL foreign keys.
Do not assume a foreign key from child to parent proves that every parent has a child.
Keep counterexamples with the model so reviewers can see what should be rejected.

takeaways: Cardinality and participation are separate constraints: maximum allowed related rows and minimum required related rows.
NOT NULL foreign keys are strong for mandatory child-to-parent relationships, but they do not by themselves enforce that every parent has at least one child.
A small counterexample dataset is an effective way to validate whether a model really specifies one-to-one, one-to-many, optional, and mandatory rules.
Use primary keys, foreign keys, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints where they match the rule; use lifecycle controls or validation for cross-row participation rules.

title: Database constraints versus validation queries
description: A practical guide for deciding which data rules belong in database constraints and which belong in validation queries, using a small hypothetical retail dataset with counterexamples.
lead: A validation query can tell you that bad data exists. A database constraint can prevent certain bad data from being committed in the first place. Treating those as interchangeable is a common modeling mistake. The practical question is not whether constraints or validation queries are better; it is which invariants must be enforced synchronously, and which possible violations can only be observed asynchronously.

sections.heading: The distinction that matters
paragraphs: A database constraint is part of the definition of a relation. It says, in effect, that some database state is not allowed. If a row would violate a primary key, foreign key, not-null rule, unique constraint, or check constraint, the database rejects the change. The bad state does not become visible as normal committed data.

A validation query is different. It reads data that already exists and returns rows that look suspicious, inconsistent, incomplete, or contrary to a business rule. It is an observation mechanism, not an enforcement mechanism. The query may run every hour, every day, before a publish step, or during a reconciliation workflow. Until it runs and someone or something responds, the violation can already affect downstream consumers.

That difference matters for data engineers because many data quality failures are misclassified. Teams sometimes use validation queries for rules that should have been enforced as relational invariants. The result is avoidable damage: orphaned facts, duplicate keys, impossible quantities, and other states that downstream models must defensively handle forever. The opposite mistake also happens: teams try to encode every operational expectation as a database constraint, even when the rule depends on time, delayed events, external systems, or a remediation process.
A useful decision rule is: enforce what makes the relation invalid by definition; validate what makes the current state suspicious, incomplete, or operationally out of policy.

The SQL examples below target PostgreSQL 18. The retail scenario is hypothetical: captured payments are compared with item totals only, excluding tax, shipping, refunds, and other adjustments. These are deliberately narrow diagnostic rules, not a complete payment reconciliation model.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail schema with enforced invariants
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order model. The core relations are customers, products, orders, and order lines. This example is intentionally small, but it is enough to separate rules that the database can enforce from rules that should be checked asynchronously.

The following definition expresses several invariants. A customer must have an email. A product must have a stock keeping unit. An order must reference an existing customer. An order line must reference an existing order and product. Quantity must be positive. A line number cannot repeat within the same order.

These rules are not merely quality preferences. If an order line refers to a product that does not exist in the modeled product relation, the line is not relationally well-formed. If quantity is negative, the row does not represent the intended kind of order line. If two rows share the same order_id and line_number, the model no longer has a stable way to identify one line within an order.
bullets: Use constraints when the rule defines whether a row or relationship is valid at all.
Prefer constraints when the rule can be decided at write time using the row and referenced keys.
Use validation queries when the rule requires observation across delayed facts, aggregates, event timing, or external business processes.

sections.heading: What constraints prevent
paragraphs: Suppose a load process tries to insert an order line with product_id 9999, but no product row has product_id 9999. With the foreign key in place, the database rejects the insert. The validation query for orphaned order lines never needs to find this case in the final table, because the invalid relationship is not allowed to exist there.

Now suppose the load process tries to insert quantity = 0 for an order line. The check constraint rejects it. Downstream logic does not need to decide whether zero means a free sample, a deleted line, a failed ingestion mapping, or an accidental default. If zero-quantity lines are meaningful in the business process, then the constraint is wrong and the model should represent that meaning explicitly. But if an order line means a purchased quantity of a product, quantity > 0 belongs in the schema.

The important point is not that every database engine has identical constraint behavior or syntax. The important modeling point is that constraints are synchronous guards on allowed states. PostgreSQL documents constraints such as check constraints, not-null constraints, unique constraints, primary keys, and foreign keys as mechanisms for defining data rules at the table level. Other relational systems expose similar concepts, although details vary.

A counterexample makes the distinction clearer. Imagine choosing not to define the product foreign key and instead scheduling this query once per day: select order lines whose product_id is missing from product. That query may be useful in a staging area. It is a poor substitute for an invariant in the final order_line table. During the day, dashboards, marts, and exports can all read the orphaned line as if it were valid. By the time the query reports the problem, the bad state has already propagated.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic query that should return no rows in a properly constrained final table.
-- Useful as a safety check, but not a substitute for the foreign key.
SELECT ol.order_id, ol.line_number, ol.product_id
FROM order_line AS ol
LEFT JOIN product AS p
  ON p.product_id = ol.product_id
WHERE p.product_id IS NULL;

sections.heading: What validation queries observe
paragraphs: Some rules are not good constraint candidates, even when they are important. They may depend on a sequence of events, a tolerance threshold, an external payment provider, or a business workflow where temporary inconsistency is expected. In those cases, a validation query is the right instrument because the purpose is to identify exceptions, not to declare the entire relation impossible.

Extend the hypothetical retail model with payment and shipment events. A payment references an order. A shipment references an order. Basic structure can still be constrained: payment amount cannot be negative, payment status must be from an allowed set, and each event must reference an existing order. But higher-level expectations require observation.

For example, a paid order should usually have at least one line. The charged amount should usually equal the sum of line quantities multiplied by unit prices. A shipment should not usually occur before the order was placed. Those are real data quality checks, but they are not the same kind of rule as quantity > 0. They compare multiple relations, aggregate line items, or interpret event timing. They may also have legitimate exceptions: a partial capture, a manual adjustment, a replacement shipment, or an order imported from an older system with incomplete event history.

Validation queries are well suited for these cases because they produce exception sets. The output should be operationally useful: order_id, the observed values, the expected values, and enough context to route the issue.

sections.heading: Worked validation exceptions
paragraphs: The next query calculates three exception types over the hypothetical schema. It is written as a diagnostic pattern rather than a claim that every retail system should use these exact rules.

The first branch finds paid orders with no order lines. The second compares captured payment amount with the computed order-line total. The third finds shipment events earlier than the order placement timestamp. Each branch returns rows that deserve investigation; it does not prove fraud, corruption, or a software defect by itself.

This distinction is important. A validation query produces candidates for review or remediation. It should be paired with an owner, severity, expected latency, and action. A daily query that nobody reads is documentation, not control. A validation query that blocks a publish step is stronger, but it is still asynchronous relative to the original write unless it runs in the same transaction as the change.

The query also illustrates why joins are central to validation. Table expressions and joins let you compare facts across relations: orders to lines, payments to computed totals, shipments to order timestamps. The relational operation is observation over current state. It does not retroactively prevent the bad state from having existed.

codeExamples.code:
WITH line_totals AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    SUM(quantity * unit_price_cents) AS line_total_cents,
    COUNT(*) AS line_count
  FROM order_line
  GROUP BY order_id
), captured_payments AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    SUM(amount_cents) AS captured_amount_cents
  FROM payment_event
  WHERE payment_status = 'captured'
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT
  'paid_order_without_lines' AS exception_type,
  o.order_id,
  NULL AS observed_cents,
  NULL AS expected_cents,
  'Paid order has no order_line rows' AS explanation
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN line_totals AS lt
  ON lt.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status = 'paid'
  AND COALESCE(lt.line_count, 0) = 0

UNION ALL

SELECT
  'captured_amount_mismatch' AS exception_type,
  o.order_id,
  cp.captured_amount_cents AS observed_cents,
  lt.line_total_cents AS expected_cents,
  'Captured payment total differs from order line total' AS explanation
FROM retail_order AS o
JOIN captured_payments AS cp
  ON cp.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN line_totals AS lt
  ON lt.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE cp.captured_amount_cents <> lt.line_total_cents

UNION ALL

SELECT
  'shipment_before_order_placed' AS exception_type,
  o.order_id,
  NULL AS observed_cents,
  NULL AS expected_cents,
  'Shipment event occurred before the order placement timestamp' AS explanation
FROM retail_order AS o
JOIN shipment_event AS se
  ON se.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE se.occurred_at < o.placed_at;

sections.heading: A decision framework for classifying rules
paragraphs: When a new data rule appears, classify it before implementing it. The classification prevents two common failures: under-enforcing structural invariants and over-constraining operational workflows.

Ask first whether the rule defines identity or referential meaning. Candidate keys, alternate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys usually belong in constraints when the modeled relationship is mandatory. If a final fact table says product_id, and product_id is supposed to refer to the product relation, enforce that reference. If the upstream feed can arrive before the product dimension, use a staging table, an unknown-product member, or a pending resolution workflow rather than weakening the final model without naming the tradeoff.

Ask next whether the rule can be evaluated at the moment of write. Not-null, check, uniqueness, and referential constraints are strong fits when the needed facts are available. Rules that require comparing today’s state with tomorrow’s file, waiting for a payment gateway, or reconciling a third-party shipment feed are usually validation checks.

Then ask whether violations are impossible or merely undesirable. Negative quantity may be impossible under the meaning of order_line. A captured amount that differs from the item total may be undesirable, but it might also reflect shipping charges, taxes, discounts, split tenders, manual credits, or a modeling omission. If legitimate exceptions exist, either refine the model so the invariant becomes precise, or keep the check as an exception report with categories.

Finally, decide what happens after detection. A constraint has a built-in consequence: reject the write. A validation query needs an operating model: alert, quarantine, backfill, annotate, suppress known exceptions, or block publication. Without that response path, the validation query only describes risk.
bullets: Constraint candidate: violation makes the row or relationship invalid by definition.
Validation candidate: violation is time-dependent, aggregate-dependent, external-system-dependent, or exception-prone.
Staging candidate: source data is allowed to be temporarily messy, but the curated relation should still enforce the invariant.

sections.heading: A practical pattern: stage, enforce, then validate
paragraphs: A robust data pipeline often uses all three layers. First, land source data with minimal assumptions in staging tables. Staging preserves evidence of what arrived, including malformed records. Second, transform into curated relational tables that enforce structural invariants. Third, run validation queries over curated data to detect business exceptions and reconciliation failures.

This pattern avoids turning final tables into unbounded error buckets. It also avoids pretending that every upstream irregularity can be solved with a check constraint. The staging layer absorbs source variability. The curated layer defines what valid relational data means. The validation layer watches for conditions that require investigation after the data becomes relationally well-formed.

For the hypothetical retail model, a staging table might accept raw order lines where product_sku is missing or quantity is a string. The curated order_line table should not. During transformation, rows that cannot be mapped to a valid product_id or positive integer quantity are rejected, quarantined, or assigned to an explicit exception workflow. Once rows enter order_line, downstream users can rely on its declared invariants.

Validation queries then handle higher-level questions: Does every paid order have lines? Do captured payments reconcile to modeled charges? Are shipment events temporally plausible? Are there orders stuck in draft for too long? These checks improve trust without weakening the core relational model.

sections.heading: Common misclassifications
paragraphs: One misclassification is using validation to replace a primary or foreign key. If a relationship is required by the model, an after-the-fact orphan check is not enough for the final table. It may still be useful as a defense-in-depth diagnostic, but it should not be the only guard.

Another misclassification is forcing uncertain business processes into rigid constraints too early. For example, shipment-before-payment may sound impossible until the business supports invoicing, subscriptions, replacements, or manual fulfillment. A premature constraint can reject legitimate records and encourage workarounds outside the model. In that case, write a validation query first, study the exception categories, and then promote the rule to a constraint only if the invariant becomes precise.

A third misclassification is hiding policy inside application code while leaving the database weaker than the model. If every application path assumes email is required, but the database allows null email in the customer relation, another loader or repair script can violate the assumption. Constraints put shared invariants where all writers must obey them.

The goal is not to maximize the number of constraints or validation queries. The goal is to make the contract explicit. Constraints define what cannot be stored as valid relational state. Validation queries define what stored state should be reviewed, reconciled, or improved.

takeaways: Use database constraints for enforced invariants: keys, required references, non-null facts, allowed domains, and checks that define whether a row or relationship is valid.
Use validation queries for asynchronously observed violations: aggregate mismatches, delayed events, temporal anomalies, reconciliation checks, and exception-prone business policies.
Do not use a scheduled validation query as the only protection for a final-table invariant that the database can enforce synchronously.
A good validation query returns actionable exception rows, not just a count. Include identifiers, observed values, expected values, and a clear exception type.
A practical pipeline separates staging tolerance, curated-table enforcement, and validation-based monitoring.
